systemOne.note: Every v1-board model re-measured on v2, plus two frontier OpenAI models through pi. gpt-6.1-sol at high thinking saturates the suite outright (800/800 — v2 has stopped measuring this tier; the remaining headroom is in harder states, not better models); gpt-6-luna at max misses only 7 records questions. The incumbent Qwen3.6-35B with reasoning enabled scores 98.6% — the same weights score 61.8% with thinking off, the widest thinking-mode gap seen on this suite. Hosted Mercury Decide (86.5%) beats hosted Jev (79.5%); Nimble-9B 68.0% as-scored (71.6% on the 380 optioned questions — its 40 open-question generations failed at transport: Ollama caps criteria at 26 vs the gateway's 64-token fallback, and no v2 open answer sits inside a 26-candidate window); Kev-4B 59.8%; Laya's non-autoregressive scorer collapses to 33.5%. Gateway limitation: its 64-candidate cap excluded the correct code on three open questions, making 6/800 responses unwinnable for every backend. Not re-measured: Kev-27B (~63 GiB), Clef-27B (~55-65 GiB) and Clef-Flash-9B (~19 GiB) do not fit beside the shared services within ~20 GiB free. These are gateway-constrained measurements; sibling questions and repeated samples are correlated. No v1 scores are included.

campaigns.question: Can frontier OpenAI models through pi beat the local winner on benchmark v2?
campaigns.answer: gpt-6.1-sol at high thinking scores 100.0% — all 800 generations, including every open records question; v2 is now saturated at the frontier. gpt-6-luna at max thinking scores 99.1% (7 misses, all records). Both run through the pi CLI per question with tools/extensions disabled; latency includes ~1 s process overhead per call. Reasoning depth, not the typed-decision transport, is what separates the top of the board.

campaigns.question: How does the whole v1 roster rank on benchmark v2?
campaigns.answer: Reasoning separates them. The incumbent Qwen3.6-35B with thinking enabled leads at 98.6% (CI 97.6–99.2) — the same weights score 61.8% with thinking off, the widest thinking-mode gap on this suite. Hosted Mercury Decide 86.5% beats hosted Jev 79.5%. Laya's scorer collapses to 33.5% (was 73.5% on v1). Kev-27B, Clef-27B and Clef-Flash-9B did not fit beside the shared services (~20 GiB free) and were not re-measured.

campaigns.question: Benchmark v2 (200 scenarios, 400 questions): does the v1 Jev↔Nimble tie still hold, and where does local Kev-4B land?
campaigns.answer: The v1 tie is gone. Jev 79.5% > Nimble-9B 68.0% as-scored (71.6% on the 380 optioned questions — its 40 open-question generations hit Ollama's 26-criteria cap) > Kev-4B 59.8%. Jev wins all ten families except policy, where Nimble edges it (85.0 vs 78.8). Kev-4B is fastest at 0.077 s/question, Nimble cheapest per answer at 1 out-token. Jev stays the s1 baseline; Nimble is the strongest local backend.

campaigns.question: Can Cloudflare's clef decision model run locally behind the s1 endpoint without disturbing what is already served?
campaigns.answer: Clef-Flash-9B — yes, cleanly. 98.0% on system1 ties Jev with an identical failure set (error_log/q1 only), and F1 1.000 on the phishing corpus at 0.47 s/email — the only local arm whose phishing noul cleared the 0.5 gate unaided on the hardest lure (0.730 vs Jev's 0.710). At ~19 GiB bf16 it ran alongside every service; nothing was stopped. The requested 27B clef (~55-65 GiB) cannot coexist with the incumbent endpoint and was not benchmarked.

campaigns.question: Can OpenRouter Mercury Decide replace the System One backend using only endpoint configuration?
campaigns.answer: Supported as an optional hosted backend, not the shared default. inception/mercury-decide:free scored 98.0% (96/98) on system1 and F1 1.000 (16/16) through the phishing pipeline, with zero generation/analyzer errors. It ties historical Jev; its advantage over today's kev-latest is within noise. Free-tier 20 requests/minute persists with a larger daily allowance: 2.64 s/question includes quota waits, 2.93 s/email. Both small datasets are saturated.

campaigns.question: Can Nimble or Laya replace Jev behind the standard s1 endpoint?
campaigns.answer: Nimble — yes. 98.0 % ties Jev over the identical gateway transport, fully local (Ollama Q8_0, ~9.5 GiB), no API key. Laya typed-decisions — no: 73.5 %, failures across 12 tasks at every difficulty.

campaigns.question: Does the swap hold on a real workload — the anti-phishing classifier?
campaigns.answer: Almost. Nimble scored 94.1 F1 vs Jev's 100 on the 16-email adjudicated corpus through the unchanged typesafe analyzer — one missed credential-harvesting lure, and its threat-type head disagrees with its own verdict on benign mail. Proven hot-spare via env vars alone, not yet a primary.

campaigns.question: Does thinking mode help a coding agent?
campaigns.answer: No for one-shot. Thinking off: same or better pass@1, ~13× fewer output tokens, ~32× lower wall-clock.

campaigns.question: Should Ornith-1.5 replace Qwen3.6-35B-A3B?
campaigns.answer: No. Ties at its best config, −20 points at the config we deploy.

campaigns.question: Does the harness around the model change the answer?
campaigns.answer: Yes, by as much as a model swap. Same model: 44.9 built-in → 68.2 claude-code on agentic-hard.

campaigns.question: Can a free stealth cloud model drive a real tool loop?
campaigns.answer: Yes. 74.8 agent score, 96.9 % solve via opencode — use thinking OFF.

campaigns.question: muse-spark-1.2 vs mimo-v2.5-free on opencode
campaigns.answer: mimo-v2.5-free wins. Isolated beats live by 12–14 points on an 8 GiB box.

campaigns.question: Should Qwen3.8-Flash-Next replace Qwen3.6 locally?
campaigns.answer: No. Wins only think-OFF (+7 pp, noise); loses think-ON and both agentic modes at 2–17× wall time.

campaigns.question: Is MiniCPM5-2B via mlx-dspark good for agentic work on M1 Max?
campaigns.answer: Usable, but not strong. Thinking OFF by default — ON costs 3.5× tokens for no real gain.

campaigns.question: Is the daily Devin CLI + SWE-2 Max setup any good?
campaigns.answer: Yes. 72.6 agent score live, +1.2 over isolated is noise. Surface was idle (1 call in 67).

campaigns.question: Latest opencode live setup (MiMo v2.6 Flash Free)
campaigns.answer: 64.5 agent, 100 % solved, 100 % valid calls. Efficiency vs par is the remaining gap.

campaigns.question: How does the daily claude-code + Opus 5.5 setup score?
campaigns.answer: Yes, top of the ledger. 100.0 agent score: 8/8 solved in 2.8 calls vs par 5.9, 74 s wall. One sample, and ~108k input tokens per task from live skills/MCP.

campaigns.question: Hosted harnesses on the new agentic-all (hidden tests sandboxed): devin SWE-2 Max vs opencode Muse Spark 1.3 Free
campaigns.answer: A tie on solving: Muse 48/48 (100 %, CI 93–100), SWE-2 Max 47/48 (97.9 %, CI 89–100; one 900 s timeout). SWE-2 Max is more efficient (77 % vs 70 %); Muse is ~1.8× faster with ~4× fewer input tokens per task. Near-saturated at 3 samples.

systemOneV1.note: Benchmark v1 reference only. Fresh local runs put both Cloudflare Clef variants at 98.0% (96/98), matching historical Jev with the same error_log/q1 misses. Their margins over current Kev-4B (95.9%, 94/98) are within uncertainty. Clef-Flash takes 0.69 s/question and fits alongside Qwen; full Clef takes 1.93 s and required pausing Qwen vLLM to fit. realUseCase.note: Clef-Flash-9B scored F1 1.000 on all 16 emails at 0.47 s/email — the only local arm whose phishing noul cleared the 0.5 analyzer gate unaided on the hardest credential-harvesting lure (0.730 vs Jev's 0.710), where both Kev variants needed the risk pipeline and Nimble missed outright. The existing typesafe_only pipeline makes the final risk decision — this is not a raw noul-head score. Jev, both Kevs, Mercury Decide and gpt-oss-120b also solved 16/16; Nimble scored 0.941. n=16 is saturated, not proof of generalization: one flip changes F1 by about 6 points.
